match.reason: No existing point teaches how expectations of rising prices feed into wages and prices to keep inflation going; e-inflation covers only demand-pull and cost-push causes, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: Inflationary expectations
card: Inflationary expectations are what people believe will happen to the general level of prices in the future. Workers, firms and consumers all form these beliefs.
If workers expect prices to rise, they ask for higher wages to protect what their pay can buy. If firms expect their costs to rise, they may lift their own prices ahead of time.
Higher wages raise firms' costs, and firms may pass them on in higher prices. This can lead workers to ask for still higher wages, so inflation can keep going.
For this reason, expectations can make inflation hold itself in place. A central bank such as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) wants people to believe inflation will stay low and steady.
draft.remember: Expecting higher prices can lead to actions that make prices rise.

a.q: Why can inflationary expectations keep inflation going?
opts: Wage claims and early price rises can lift costs and prices
Higher prices make workers expect lower wages in future
Firms cut prices when they expect prices to rise
Consumers spend less now because they expect prices to fall
a.why: If people expect rising prices, they ask for higher wages and firms lift prices, and this can push prices up as expected. The reverse of these actions would not keep inflation going.
a.clue: Think about what workers and firms do when they expect prices to rise.

b.q: Workers at a bakery chain in Perth expect prices to rise by 5% next year. What are they most likely to do?
opts: Ask for a pay rise of about 5% or more
Accept a pay cut to help the firm
Ask for pay to stay the same
Leave work to avoid rising prices
b.why: Workers who expect prices to rise want pay that keeps up, so they ask for higher wages. Accepting the same or less pay would lower what their wages can buy, which does not fit their expectation.
b.clue: What would protect what their pay can buy?

a.best: Wage claims and early price rises can lift costs and prices

b.best: Ask for a pay rise of about 5% or more

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a precise detail ("about 5% or more"), and it echoes the 5% in the question. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

b.q: Workers at a bakery chain in Perth expect prices to rise next year. They win a pay rise, and the firm passes the cost on in higher prices. What can happen next?
opts: Workers seek higher wages again, so inflation keeps going
Prices rise once, then inflation stops of its own accord
Workers' pay now buys more, so price rises slow down
The firm's costs fall, so it can lower its prices
b.why: Once the firm lifts its prices, the pay rise buys little more than before, so workers can ask for still higher wages. Each round lifts costs and prices again, so inflation can keep going. Thinking prices rise once and then stop misses how the price rise feeds new wage claims.
b.clue: Does the cycle have to end with the firm's price rise?
